descriptions.home: Code survives; context does not. Ontology Atlas keeps your project's context (what depends on what, and why it was built this way) in one markdown folder. Prose a person can read, and a structure an AI agent reads and writes over MCP. Local-first, no backend, open source.
descriptions.download: Free desktop app. Open a markdown folder on your own disk as a project map, and connect Claude Code, Codex or Cursor over MCP. macOS is signed and notarized; the Windows x64 beta states its unsigned status before download.
descriptions.topology: See your project's domains, capabilities, elements and their dependencies as one map. Markdown frontmatter is the graph, and the files stay on your own disk.
descriptions.docs: Read and edit the markdown folder directly. Change the frontmatter and the map follows.
descriptions.projects: Every project and hub on this map, with the domains and capabilities each one is made of.
descriptions.ontologyStudio: Put one node at the center and fill its four bearings: broader, contains, depends on, relates to. What you fill is written straight into markdown frontmatter.
descriptions.ontologyInsights: Node census by kind, the hubs with the most connections, and the nodes still attached to nothing. Where to look before you grow the map.
descriptions.guide: Getting started with Ontology Atlas: turn a markdown folder into a map, and connect Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor over MCP.
descriptions.changelog: Ontology Atlas changelog: user-visible changes, newest first.

welcome.title: This map comes from documents
welcome.body: Every dot here is either one real markdown file, or something one of those files names. The whole map is a single picture of what our product is made of and how the pieces connect. A picture like this is called an ontology: the name sounds academic, but that one sentence is all it means. Takes about 2 minutes.

nodes.title: Size and shape of the dots
nodes.body: The biggest dot is the whole product, the next size down is an area, and the small dots are individual features and parts. A dot's shape tells you what it is.

relations.title: Lines are relationships
relations.body: A solid line means "contained in", a dashed line means "depends on". The legend here always reminds you.

tryClick.title: Try clicking one
tryClick.body: Click the dot that's still bright on the map. Its story (what it is and what it connects to) opens in a card.

datasheet.title: The card is the front of the document
datasheet.body: Everything in this card comes straight from that markdown file. Edit here and the file changes; edit the file and this changes.

index.title: INDEX: the map's table of contents
index.body: If the map is a picture, INDEX is a list. It's the fastest way to find something by name.

recent.title: What changed recently
recent.body: Flip this switch and only the recently changed stuff stays bright. Good place to start when you're coming back after a while.

agent.title: Growing it together with an AI agent
agent.body: Coding agents like Claude Code can read and write this map. One command in the INDEX starter card builds this map from your own codebase.

docsWhat.title: Open a dot and you land here
docsWhat.body: A dot on the map is one piece of writing here. This is where you read it, edit it, and write new ones. What you change here is saved straight into the files on your computer.

docsList.title: Your folder, listed on the left
docsList.body: Everything in the folder shows up here. Click to open, and keep several open as tabs. Pick your own folder up top and your own writing shows up instead.

studioWhat.title: A bench for joining pieces together
studioWhat.body: You wrote the piece, but what it is part of and what it leans on are often still blank. This is where you fill those blanks in, one at a time. Every blank you fill adds a line to the map.

studioCard.title: The card in the middle is the piece you're on
studioCard.body: Each of its four edges is one blank. Click a dashed edge to choose what fills it, and a filled edge turns solid. Fill them and it saves straight into the file in your folder.

insightsWhat.title: Where you check the whole thing
insightsWhat.body: As the pile grows, some pieces end up connected to nothing and some go untouched for months. This finds all of that in one place. Start here when you don't know what to tidy up first.

insightsToday.title: What to fix today, first
insightsToday.body: The few things that help most right now sit at the top. Click one to check it on the map, or go straight to fixing it.

projectsWhat.title: Grouped by product
projectsWhat.body: Documents that name a product stand as cards here. The bars show how that product splits into areas, and how each area balances claims (capabilities) against evidence (elements).

projectsCard.title: One card, one product
projectsCard.body: Each bar shows how that area splits between claims (capabilities) and evidence (elements). Size is on the right, as a number. Open the card for detail, or jump straight to that spot on the map.

gitWhat.title: A record of what changed, and when
gitWhat.body: Every edit you make piles up here. You can also save the whole current state so you can look back later, or go back to it. Only the writing in this folder is touched.

gitChanges.title: Start with what changed
gitChanges.body: Everything you edited is listed here. Look it over, then save it and that moment is on the record. In a browser you can look; install the app and you can save from here too.

agentsWhat.title: Connect your AI coding tools here
agentsWhat.body: Atlas launches the tools installed on this computer so you can talk to them right here. If one is missing you can fetch it from here. It lands in an app-only folder and goes away with the app.

agentsCheck.title: If nothing connects, measure it here
agentsCheck.body: “Check again” re-scans this computer. Each tool also has its own connection check that measures where things are stuck, step by step, and repairs what it can.

The bar shows how those split between capabilities and elements: capabilities on the left, elements on the right. A bar leaning hard one way means claims without evidence, or the reverse. auth.title: An old app-scoped sign-in is getting in the way
auth.hint: You do not need a separate sign-in. This app uses the same one you use in your terminal. What is in the way is a keychain entry from an earlier app-scoped sign-in: it shadows the shared one and has already expired. Press 「New chat」 and the app clears that entry and falls back to your real sign-in. If that still fails, paste the one-line command under 「Details」 into a terminal.

install.title: A broken piece from an interrupted download is in the way
install.hint: The first-run download was cut off halfway, and the leftover pieces make it fail at the same spot every time. Press “New chat” and the app clears them and downloads again from scratch. Check your internet connection and keep the app open while it downloads (a few hundred MB).

bootstrap.label: Read the code and start the map
bootstrap.prompt: Read this repository and propose candidate domains and capabilities. Cite the file paths you based each on, and write nothing to the vault until I confirm.

island.label: {count} nodes around “{first}” sit apart from the map
island.prompt: {count} nodes including “{first}” are not connected to the rest of the map. Using the code as evidence, work out where they belong and propose the links along with why.

containment.label: “{domain}” does not link back to “{slug}”
containment.prompt: “{slug}” says it belongs to “{domain}”, but “{domain}” does not list it. Check whether that is right, and link it if so.

evidence.label: {count} capabilities with no code behind them
evidence.prompt: {count} capabilities including “{first}” have no implementation evidence. Find which file each one actually lives in and record it. Say so when you cannot find one.

explain.label: Explain this folder from the map alone
explain.prompt: Using only the {count} nodes on the map and their relations, explain to a newcomer what this folder is. Invent nothing that is not on the map, and point out any place the explanation stalls, because that is a hole in the map.
